title: Understanding Goal Generalisation in Sequential Reinforcement Learning
claim: We formalise how training histories map to out-of-distribution behaviour, and test predicted preferences against empirical ones.
layout: 2 panels; left concrete grid-world flow, right abstract commutative diagram
description: The left panel shows the experimental design. Two grayed grid-world boxes (Stage 1 and Stage 2) show an agent heading to a red diamond, then to a red cross, joined by gray arrows. A highlighted orange Evaluation grid follows, with a red plus and a blue cross and a '?' start marker. A brace under the training stages leads to a dashed teal arrow labelled 'latent policy gradient', which points to a teal box with predicted preference bars (71% plus, 29% cross). A dashed orange arrow from Evaluation leads to an orange box with empirical bars (73% and 27%). A double-headed arrow links the two boxes. The right panel is a square commutative diagram. Training pipeline Ω goes to Agent π̂_Ω by Training. Ω goes to Predicted Π_Ω by Modelling. The Agent goes to Induced Π̂_Ω by Rollout. The two preferences are compared with KL divergence.
caption: Left: Illustration of our experimental design. Our experimental design is covered in [ref]. RL agents are trained on pipelines involving either one or two stages (e.g., trained to pursue \sym{red}{diamond} in stage 1 and \sym{red}{cross} in stage 2). They are then evaluated in out-of-distribution environments containing two objects (e.g., \sym{red}{plus} and \sym{blue}{cross}) to generate an empirical preference distribution. We explore these distributions in [ref]. Then, in [ref], we introduce a method of predicting preference from training pipelines---the latent policy gradients method---and compare the fit between the predicted and empirical preferences. Right: The goal generalisation modelling problem. Training pipelines are used to train agents, which are then rolled out in evaluation environments to produce an induced preference function. Modelling gives predicted preference functions. We find the fit of our model by comparing the average KL-divergence between the predicted and induced preference functions.
abstract: Reinforcement learning agents often exhibit unintended goal-directed behaviour outside their training distribution, but we currently lack a principled understanding of how such agents will generalise to novel environments based on their training history. We address this gap for agents trained sequentially on one or more tasks. We study over 100 sequential training pipelines, evaluating behaviour across over 250 out-of-distribution environments. We find that salient features drive generalisation, and that goals learnt early in training can persist and influence those acquired later. To explain these phenomena, we introduce latent policy gradients, a method that predicts what out-of-distribution behaviour a training pipeline will likely induce. Our method simulates the evolution of low-dimensional latent variables during training according to what would achieve high reward on the training objective with respect to a simple model of how the latent variables map to behaviour. It achieves strong predictive accuracy, generalises to unseen types of training pipeline, and is interpretable. Our findings demonstrate that while out-of-distribution RL agent behaviour is dependent on the whole training pipeline, this dependence has an underlying structure we can capture, laying groundwork for understanding goal generalisation from a developmental perspective.
